# Classes and objects

robjc declares classes using R6 **class generators** and creates instances with their `$new()` methods.
The generator holds information such as the class name and parent class. An instance refers to that information to determine its own class.
This guide builds a small class to explore initialization, inheritance, and reference identity.

## Define an ordinary class

`RSObjectClass()` is the factory for an ordinary robjc class.
Pass the parent class generator as `super_class`; omitting it inherits from `RSObject`.
Use `private` for internal state and `public` for externally accessible methods and values.
A member cannot have the same name in both `private` and `public`.

```{r}
library(robjc)

Record <- RSObjectClass(
  "Guide02Record",
  super_class = RSObject,
  private = list(.label = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(label) {
      super$initialize()
      if (!is.character(label) || length(label) != 1L || is.na(label))
        return(NULL)
      private$.label <- label
      invisible(self)
    },
    label = function() private$.label
  )
)
```

`Record` is a class generator, not an instance.
`private$.label` is state held by each instance; the public `label()` method provides access to it.
See the [Class Factory Guide](guide_05_ClassFactory.Rmd) for the factory arguments and other kinds of classes.

## Create and initialize an instance

robjc's `Class$new(...)` allocates an instance and then calls `initialize(...)`.
**`$new()` returns the value returned by `initialize()`.**
Return `self` after successfully constructing a usable instance. Using `invisible(self)` also suppresses automatic display in an interactive session.

The `initialize()` above first calls `super$initialize()` to run its parent's initialization.
It then validates `label`, stores a valid value, and returns `self`.
If validation fails, it returns `NULL`, so `$new()` also returns `NULL`.

When implementing `initialize()` in a custom class, pay attention to two points:

**1. Call `super$initialize()`:**
The base class `RSObject` sets the instance's S3 class in its `initialize()` method.
Calling `super$initialize()` ensures that initialization performed by parent classes runs as well.

**2. Explicitly return the intended value, usually `self`:**
Unlike ordinary R6 `new()`, robjc's `$new()` returns the result of `initialize()` directly.
You can return `NULL` when initialization fails, but avoid accidentally returning an unintended value from the last expression.

```{r}
record <- Record$new("first")
stopifnot(record$isMemberOf(Record))
stopifnot(identical(record$label(), "first"))

invalid <- Record$new(1L)
stopifnot(is.null(invalid))
```

## Inspect class relationships

An instance's `class()` returns its class **generator**, and `superclass()` returns the generator for its immediate parent.
This differs from base R's `class(object)`, which returns a character vector of class names.
`isMemberOf(Class)` checks direct membership, while `isKindOf(Class)` also includes ancestors.

```{r}
TaggedRecord <- RSObjectClass(
  "Guide02TaggedRecord",
  super_class = Record,
  public = list(tag = function() "tagged")
)

tagged <- TaggedRecord$new("second")
stopifnot(identical(tagged$class(), TaggedRecord))
stopifnot(identical(tagged$superclass(), Record))
stopifnot(tagged$isMemberOf(TaggedRecord))
stopifnot(!tagged$isMemberOf(Record))
stopifnot(tagged$isKindOf(Record))
stopifnot(tagged$isKindOf(RSObject))
stopifnot(identical(tagged$label(), "second"))
```

Pass a generator such as `Record` to these checks, not a name such as `"Guide02Record"`.
Two declarations can use the same name and still create distinct classes, so the name alone does not establish class identity.

## Work with reference identity

robjc instances are reference objects.
Assigning one to another variable creates another reference to the same instance; calling `$new()` again creates a separate instance.
`identical()` and robjc's `==` and `!=` compare this **reference identity**.

```{r}
alias <- record
another <- Record$new("first")

stopifnot(identical(record, alias))
stopifnot(record == alias)
stopifnot(record != another)
stopifnot(!identical(record, another))
```

`record` and `another` hold the same string, but they are separate instances.
Use `isEqual()` to ask whether objects are equal as values.
This `Record` class does not define its own `isEqual()`, so it inherits the base behavior and is unequal to another instance.
The [Identity, Equality, and Hashing Guide](guide_08_Hash_isEqual.Rmd) explains how to define value-based equality.

```{r}
stopifnot(!record$isEqual(another))
stopifnot(record$isEqual(alias))
```

## Describe and copy an object

`description()` returns the same layout as S3 `print()`, showing public and private data but omitting methods.
`debugDescription()` adds public and private methods to that layout.
Both return display text rather than a storage format.

```{r}
ordinary <- record$description()
details <- record$debugDescription()

stopifnot(grepl("Guide02Record", ordinary, fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(grepl(".label", details, fixed = TRUE))
stopifnot(grepl("label", details, fixed = TRUE))
```

The base class `RSObject` returns `self` from `copy()`.
Thus, `Record$copy()` also returns the same instance.
If a class needs an independent copy, override `copy()` and decide what to duplicate and what to share.
Not every class provides `mutableCopy()`. Collections and Vectors that have corresponding mutable classes provide it.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(record$copy(), record))
stopifnot(!record$respondsTo("mutableCopy"))

fixed_array <- RSArray$new(list(record))
editable_array <- fixed_array$mutableCopy()
stopifnot(editable_array$isMemberOf(RSMutableArray))
stopifnot(identical(editable_array$objectAtIndex(1L), record))
```

Copying an Array creates a separate outer collection but retains a reference to the same `record`.
The [Values and Copying Guide](guide_06_Values_Copying.Rmd) covers copy depth and custom implementations.
